review_status: DRAFT. Every item needs sign-off from a Grade 9 subject teacher (maths, natural sciences, English) before learners see it. Item statistics from the pilot (norming job) decide which items stay.
notes: Each check is built from units (one CAPS topic each, in rising difficulty). One variant per unit is served, chosen at random per learner, so two learners side by side rarely see the same question. 'answer' is the index of the correct option as written; options are shuffled per learner when shown. Answer keys never leave the server.

reading.title: Reading check
reading.intro: Two short texts, four questions each. Every Grade 10 subject is taught and tested in English, so this tells us something about all of them. Read at your own pace.

passage.title: Gogo's spaza
passage.text:
Every afternoon after school, Ayanda helps at her gogo's spaza shop in Mamelodi. For months, bread and airtime sold well, but in March the bread sales dropped by almost half. Gogo blamed the weather. Ayanda was not so sure.

She started writing down every sale in an old exercise book: what was bought, and at what time. After two weeks she noticed something. Before 7 a.m., almost no bread was sold any more. That was exactly when the new bakery van started stopping at the taxi rank two streets away, selling bread for R2 less.

Ayanda did not suggest dropping the price. Instead, she asked her gogo to open thirty minutes earlier and to sell bread with a hot cup of tea for the price of the bread alone. Within a month, the morning queue was back — and now the regulars stayed to talk.

items.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A learner who solves a business problem by looking carefully at evidence
Why bakeries are better than spaza shops
How bad weather affects bread sales
A grandmother who refuses to change

items.stem: Why did morning bread sales drop?
options: The weather was bad in March
A bakery van nearby sold bread for less

items.stem: Why did Ayanda probably NOT suggest cutting the bread price?
options: She wanted to compete in a way the van couldn't easily copy
Bread prices are fixed by law

items.stem: "Ayanda was not so sure." What does this sentence tell us?
options: She was confused about the weather
She was unsure whether to keep helping

passage.title: Day Zero
passage.text:
In 2017 and early 2018, after three dry winters in a row, Cape Town's dams fell to their lowest levels in decades. The city warned that if dam levels kept falling, it would reach "Day Zero": the day most taps would be turned off and people would collect a daily ration of water at collection points.

To push that day back, households were asked to use no more than 50 litres per person a day — less than one five-minute shower. People reused bath water to flush toilets, farmers released water to the city, and the government limited how much water businesses could use.

Day Zero never came. Water use in the city fell to about half of what it had been, and good winter rains in 2018 began to refill the dams. Many people kept some of their new habits even after the restrictions were lifted.

items.stem: What was "Day Zero"?
options: The day most taps would be turned off
The first day of the 2018 rains

items.stem: Why does the writer compare 50 litres to a five-minute shower?
options: To show how small the daily limit was
To recommend showering for five minutes
To prove that showers waste water

items.stem: According to the passage, which TWO things together helped Cape Town avoid Day Zero?
options: Businesses closing and people leaving the city
Lower water use and winter rains
Farmers using more water and fewer showers

items.stem: What does the last sentence suggest?
options: People forgot about the drought quickly
The crisis changed some people's behaviour for good
Water use went back up immediately

passage.title: Phones belong in the classroom
passage.text:
Many schools ban cellphones in class. I think that is a mistake.

For learners whose families can't afford data at home, school wi-fi on a phone may be the only way to watch a maths video or check a word in a dictionary app. A ban takes that away from the learners who need it most.

Of course, phones can distract. Some learners will scroll social media instead of working. But that is a reason to teach learners when phones help and when they don't — not a reason to pretend phones don't exist. After school, every job and university course will expect us to use them well.

A better rule would be simple: phones face-down unless the teacher says they're needed. That keeps the benefits and limits the distraction.

items.stem: What is the writer's main claim?
options: Banning phones in class is a mistake

items.stem: In the third paragraph, why does the writer admit that phones can distract?
options: To deal with the strongest argument against them
To prove phones should be banned

items.stem: Which reason does the writer give for allowing phones?
options: Some learners have no other way to get online

items.stem: Which statement is an OPINION rather than a fact?
options: Many schools ban cellphones in class
Some learners will scroll social media
School wi-fi can be used on a phone

passage.title: Should school start later?
passage.text:
Our school starts at 7:30. I believe it should start at 8:30.

Scientists who study sleep have found that during the teenage years the body clock shifts, so many teenagers only feel sleepy late at night. When school starts early, they arrive tired. Tired learners find it harder to concentrate and remember what they learn.

Some parents say a later start would make it harder for them to drop children off before work. That is a real problem, and schools would need to keep the gates open early for learners who arrive with their parents.

But a school day should be designed around how learners learn best. An extra hour of sleep costs nothing, and it may be one of the cheapest ways to improve marks.

items.stem: What does the writer want?
options: Parents to drive learners to school

items.stem: What evidence does the writer use to support their view?
How does the writer respond to the parents' concern?
options: They accept it and suggest a solution

items.stem: "one of the cheapest ways to improve marks" — what is the writer suggesting?
options: A later start could help learners at almost no cost
